audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation (Paul 1918 Cap. II ss.8, 10, 11-13, 15, pp. 11-14) is verbatim in the scanned file we hold at the stated pages. (2) The source is the standard reference grammar of Middle High German, not a primer; the Glottolog list contains only pedagogical works that rank below it, and for a historical language no instrumental/JIPA-type study can exist. (3) An independent open handbook downloaded now (Wright 1907 Historical German Grammar s.24 p. 19, states the same rule: chief stress on the stem syllable, always the first syllable; secondary stress fluctuating -- confirming both the primary rule and Paul's rejection of a quantity-based nebenton rule. (4) Only improvement available is citing the 2007 25th edition of Paul (paywalled), which would modernize the citation but is not expected to alter the classification. web search bud

sources.citation: Joseph Wright, Historical German Grammar, vol. I: Phonology, Word-Formation and Accidence. Oxford: OUP 1907 (archive.org historicalgerman01wriguoft, scanned text).
sources.quote: s.24: 'The rule for the accentuation of uncompounded words is the same in German as in the other Germanic languages, viz. the chief stress falls upon the stem-syllable and always remains there even when suffixes and inflexional endings follow it. This syllable is always the first of the word. The position of the secondary stress in trisyllabic and polysyllabic words fluctuated in OHG. and MHG. just as it does in NHG.' s.25: compound verbs with inseparable first element stress the second element; nominal compounds stress the first.
